lessons.title: View Controller Lifecycle & Containment
lessons.body:
Every UIViewController moves through a predictable sequence of lifecycle methods. Understanding when each fires — and what work belongs there — prevents subtle bugs.

**The sequence on first presentation:**
1. `loadView` — UIKit creates (or you manually assign) `self.view`. Rarely overridden unless you want a fully custom root view.
2. `viewDidLoad` — called **once**, after the view is in memory. This is the right place for one-time setup: adding subviews, installing Auto Layout constraints, configuring data sources.
3. `viewWillAppear(_:)` — called before **each** appearance. Use it for work that must refresh on re-entry: starting animations, re-subscribing to notifications, updating data that may have changed.
4. `viewDidAppear(_:)` — view is on screen. Start timers or analytics here.
5. `viewWillDisappear(_:)` — about to leave screen. Stop animations, save drafts.
6. `viewDidDisappear(_:)` — off screen. Release resources tied to visibility.

**Key rule:** layout code (addSubview, NSLayoutConstraint) lives in `viewDidLoad`; appearance-driven animations live in `viewWillAppear`/`viewWillDisappear`.

**Containment** extends this lifecycle to container view controllers (e.g. a custom tab or paging controller) that host other view controllers as children. Adding a child correctly takes three steps: call `addChild(_:)`, add the child's `view` as a subview, then call `didMove(toParent:)` once the child is fully installed. Skipping `didMove(toParent:)` — or calling it before the child's view is actually in the hierarchy — leaves the child improperly installed even though it's visible on screen.

```swift
class ProfileViewController: UIViewController {
    private let avatarView = UIImageView()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        view.addSubview(avatarView)
        NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
            avatarView.centerXAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.centerXAnchor),
            avatarView.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor, constant: 24)
        ])
    }

    override func viewWillAppear(_ animated: Bool) {
        super.viewWillAppear(animated)
        avatarView.image = currentUser.avatar
    }
}
```

quickCheck.prompt: Which method is called exactly once when the view controller's view is first loaded into memory?
quickCheck.explanation: viewDidLoad fires a single time after the view hierarchy is loaded. viewWillAppear and viewDidAppear fire on every appearance, and loadView is for creating the view itself — not responding to it being loaded.

options.text: viewWillAppear
viewDidAppear
viewDidLoad
loadView

lessons.title: Auto Layout, Constraints & UIStackView
lessons.body:
Auto Layout solves view positioning by satisfying a system of linear constraints at runtime, adapting to any screen size or orientation.

**Core concepts:**
- **NSLayoutConstraint** represents a linear equation: `item1.attribute = multiplier × item2.attribute + constant`.
- **`translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false`** — set this on any view you constrain programmatically, or you'll get conflicts.
- **Intrinsic content size** — views like `UILabel` and `UIButton` know their natural size from content.
- **Content Hugging Priority (CHP)** — how strongly a view resists growing *beyond* its intrinsic size.
- **Compression Resistance Priority (CRP)** — how strongly a view resists shrinking *below* its intrinsic size.
- **Ambiguous layouts** appear when constraints don't fully determine position or size — several results satisfy them equally. **Unsatisfiable layouts** occur when constraints actively conflict, and UIKit logs a warning while breaking one of them.

**UIStackView** arranges a row or column of views without you hand-writing constraints between them: it derives spacing and sizing from its `axis`, `distribution`, `spacing`, and `alignment` properties. It's still Auto Layout underneath — each arranged view's intrinsic size and priorities still matter — it just saves you from maintaining the constraints yourself.

```swift
let label = UILabel()
label.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
view.addSubview(label)

NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
    label.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
    label.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.trailingAnchor, constant: -16),
    label.centerYAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.centerYAnchor)
])
label.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.required, for: .horizontal)
```

quickCheck.prompt: What property must you set to false before adding programmatic Auto Layout constraints to a view?
quickCheck.explanation: UIKit generates implicit constraints from a view's autoresizingMask unless you opt out. Setting translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints to false removes those implicit constraints so your manual ones can work without conflicts.

options.text: clipsToBounds
translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints
isHidden
autoresizingMask

lessons.title: Responder Chain, Target-Action & Delegation

quickCheck.prompt: Why should a delegate property be declared `weak`?
quickCheck.explanation: The delegating object is usually owned by its delegate (e.g. a VC owns its subview). If the subview held a strong reference back to the VC, both objects would keep each other alive indefinitely — a retain cycle. weak breaks the cycle.

options.text: Because delegates are always declared as value types in UIKit, never reference types
Because UIKit requires it for all stored properties on a view controller
To improve rendering performance
To break the retain cycle between delegate and delegating object

lessons.title: Cell Reuse, Diffable Data Sources & SwiftUI Interop
lessons.body:
UITableView and UICollectionView keep memory bounded by reusing cell objects rather than allocating one per row. `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:)` pulls a cell from a per-identifier pool — if none is free, the pool creates one, but a cell built earlier for a completely different row can come back with its old content still attached.

That's why cells reset their own state — typically in `prepareForReuse()`, or right when new data is bound — before showing anything new: image views must clear a placeholder before a fresh async image load starts, any in-flight request for the *previous* row must be cancelled, and selection/highlight state must be reset. Skipping this produces the classic flash-of-wrong-content-then-correction bug during fast scrolling.

**Diffable data sources** (`UITableViewDiffableDataSource`/`UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource`) replace manual `reloadData()`/`performBatchUpdates(_:)` bookkeeping. You build an `NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot` describing the *target* state and call `apply(_:animatingDifferences:)`; the data source diffs it against the current snapshot and animates only the rows that actually changed, inserted, or moved, instead of matching index paths to your own model mutations by hand.

**Interop with SwiftUI:** `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` wrap a UIKit view or view controller for use inside a SwiftUI hierarchy, and a plain SwiftUI view can be hosted inside UIKit via `UIHostingController`. Because UIKit's delegate pattern doesn't map onto SwiftUI's value-type world, a nested `Coordinator` class is the conventional bridge — it conforms to the UIKit delegate protocol and forwards callbacks into SwiftUI bindings or closures it holds.

quickCheck.prompt: A custom UITableViewCell shows a downloaded avatar in an image view. What must it do to avoid briefly showing a stale avatar when the cell is recycled for a different row?
quickCheck.explanation: Because dequeued cells keep whatever their previous row last set, the cell needs to reset or reassign the image view's content — and cancel any in-flight load for the old row — typically in prepareForReuse or right when new data is bound.

options.text: Reset the image view's content in prepareForReuse, or right when new data binds
Nothing — dequeueReusableCell already clears all subview state before returning the cell
Call reloadData() after configuring each cell to force a brand-new instance
Register a uniquely named cell class per row so no two rows ever share an instance

questions.prompt: On first presentation, a view controller's view hasn't appeared on screen yet. Which lifecycle sequence actually fires, in order?
questions.explanation: viewDidLoad runs once, right after the view hierarchy is built. viewWillAppear then fires just before the view is actually placed on screen, and viewDidAppear right after it becomes visible — that ordering holds on every presentation, first time included.

options.text: viewWillAppear, then viewDidLoad, then viewDidAppear
loadView, then viewDidAppear, then viewWillAppear
viewDidAppear, then viewWillAppear, then viewDidLoad
viewDidLoad, then viewWillAppear, then viewDidAppear

questions.prompt: A view's frame is CGRect(x: 40, y: 100, width: 200, height: 80). What does its bounds look like, assuming no scrolling or transform is applied?
questions.explanation: frame places the view inside its superview's coordinate system. bounds describes the view's own internal coordinate system, which starts at (0,0) unless something like a scroll offset shifts it. Width and height normally match between the two; only the origin differs.

options.text: CGRect(x: 40, y: 100, width: 200, height: 80) — bounds and frame describe the same rectangle
CGRect(x: -40, y: -100, width: 200, height: 80) — bounds mirrors frame's origin
CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 200, height: 80) — bounds uses the view's own coordinate space
CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 400, height: 160) — bounds doubles frame's size for Retina scaling

questions.prompt: A table view has 5,000 rows but only ever shows about 12 on screen at once. What problem does dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:) solve here?
questions.explanation: Reuse means a small, bounded number of cell objects — roughly however many fit on screen plus a buffer — get recycled as different rows scroll into view, rather than the table view allocating thousands of cell instances up front.

options.text: It preloads all 5,000 rows' cells into memory so scrolling never allocates
It guarantees a row's cell keeps a stable identity matching a database primary key
It recycles a small pool of cells instead of allocating a new one per row
It compresses off-screen cells into a lighter placeholder format to save memory

questions.prompt: A storyboard-connected @IBOutlet property on a view controller is declared weak. What would actually change if it were declared strong instead?
questions.explanation: The view hierarchy (superview to subviews) already keeps a strong reference to every installed subview. weak just avoids the outlet being a second, redundant owner — declaring it strong here wouldn't itself create a retain cycle, since the view controller isn't part of the chain the view retains.

options.text: Interface Builder rejects the connection entirely, accepting only weak outlets
The app crashes on launch from having two strong references to one view
The outlet starts updating automatically whenever the underlying view resizes
Little changes — the view hierarchy already retains the subview strongly

questions.prompt: Why must UIKit view and layout code run on the main thread?
questions.explanation: UIKit was designed as a single-threaded framework — its view and layout internals assume only one thread touches them at a time. Unsynchronized concurrent access from another thread is what actually produces the crashes and rendering glitches, not a compiler rule, a storage detail, or a networking restriction.

options.text: UIKit's view and layout internals assume only one thread touches them
Swift's compiler rejects any UIResponder call made outside the main thread
Auto Layout constraints live in a database only the main thread can read
Background threads in iOS are limited to networking APIs only

questions.prompt: Two constraints on the same view conflict — one is required, one has priority 500. What does Auto Layout do at layout time?
questions.explanation: Priority (1–1000) tells Auto Layout how much a constraint may be sacrificed under conflict. A required constraint holds; anything below it gives way rather than producing a layout the system can't resolve.

options.text: It throws a fatal error — only one constraint may ever target a given attribute
It breaks the 500-priority constraint and keeps the required one intact
It averages the two constraints' requested values into one blended result
It drops both constraints and falls back on the view's intrinsic content size

questions.prompt: A custom UIView overrides layoutSubviews() to reposition two child views by hand. Under what circumstance does that override actually run?
questions.explanation: layoutSubviews fires whenever the view genuinely needs a fresh layout pass — a bounds change, or a deferred (setNeedsLayout) or immediate (layoutIfNeeded) request. It isn't tied to a timer, a one-time first load, or the drawing-specific needsDisplay flag.

options.text: Only the very first time the view is ever added to a window, and never on any later bounds change
On a fixed timer UIKit runs alongside the display refresh
Whenever the bounds change or setNeedsLayout()/layoutIfNeeded() is called
Only when the view explicitly sets needsDisplay = true

questions.prompt: A tap lands on a UIButton nested inside several superviews, none of which handle the touch themselves. Where does the responder chain look for a handler after the button, if the button doesn't consume the event?
questions.explanation: The chain climbs from the hit-tested responder upward: superview by superview, then the containing view controller, the window, and finally the application — each link gets a chance before the event is discarded.

options.text: Up through each superview, then the view controller, window, and app
Down into the button's own subviews before considering anything above
Directly to the app delegate, bypassing any view controller in between
Back to whichever view most recently called becomeFirstResponder()

questions.prompt: A UITableView's data source implements numberOfRowsInSection returning 0 for every section — so cellForRowAt is never invoked, even though it's implemented too — while the delegate's tableView(_:didSelectRowAt:) is implemented. What happens?
questions.explanation: DataSource methods (numberOfRowsInSection, cellForRowAt) are what actually produce rows and their content. Returning 0 rows means cellForRowAt never runs, so nothing is on screen. Delegate methods like didSelectRowAt only react to interaction with rows that already exist — with a row count of zero, there's nothing on screen to select in the first place.

options.text: The table view shows no rows at all, since nothing exists for didSelectRowAt to be called on
The table view falls back to a single default row, treating didSelectRowAt as enough to render it
It crashes at launch — UITableViewDelegate methods require a matching data source method to exist
The rows render correctly — delegate and data source are just two names for one protocol

questions.prompt: A UILabel with a long line of text has no explicit width or height constraints, just leading/top constraints pinning its position. How does Auto Layout decide its size?
questions.explanation: Views like UILabel and UIButton can report a natural size — intrinsicContentSize — derived from their content. Auto Layout uses that as an implicit constraint whenever no explicit width/height is given.

options.text: It fills 100% of the superview's remaining width and height
It sizes to zero until an explicit width or height constraint appears
It asks the label for its intrinsicContentSize based on text and font
It inherits the frame of whichever sibling view was added just before it

questions.prompt: A container view controller adds a child's view as a subview but never calls didMove(toParent:). What goes wrong?
questions.explanation: didMove(toParent:) is the signal that containment is complete. Skipping it leaves the child improperly installed — its view can be visible, but it never receives the full containment lifecycle callbacks the system expects for it.

options.text: The child's view fails to render until the app is relaunched
Auto Layout refuses to activate constraints on the child's view
The parent crashes the next time it deallocates, its child array corrupted by the dangling reference
The child never receives the callbacks marking it as properly installed

questions.prompt: What triggers handleLogin() to run in this view controller?
questions.explanation: addTarget(_:action:for:) registers self and a selector against a specific control event. When that event — touchUpInside here — occurs, UIKit sends the message directly; no closures, KVO, or plist entries are involved.

options.text: SwiftUI's action-closure mechanism, which UIButton bridges to automatically
UIKit sends the handleLogin selector to self when touchUpInside fires
A KVO observation registered implicitly by addTarget(_:action:for:)
Nothing runs unless handleLogin is listed in Info.plist as an exported selector

questions.prompt: Scrolling fast through a list of avatars, a cell sometimes briefly shows a different user's photo before correcting itself. What's missing from this cell?
questions.explanation: Because cells are reused, an image-loading closure kicked off for row A can still be in flight when the cell is recycled for row B. Without cancelling that earlier request — typically in prepareForReuse — its completion handler fires late and overwrites row B's image with row A's result.

options.text: Calling reloadData() at the start of configure(with:) to rebuild the cell
Marking avatarView as weak so it can't retain a stale image
Registering the cell class with register(_:forCellReuseIdentifier:) instead of an outlet
Cancelling the prior row's in-flight image load, e.g. in prepareForReuse()

questions.prompt: A row of three labels needs even horizontal spacing and should adapt automatically as one label's text changes length. What's the main advantage of a UIStackView over hand-written NSLayoutConstraints here?
questions.explanation: UIStackView still uses Auto Layout underneath — it just derives and manages the constraints between its arranged views from axis/distribution/spacing/alignment, which is why adding, removing, or resizing arranged views doesn't require rewriting constraints by hand.

options.text: It derives spacing and sizing constraints from its axis and distribution
It bypasses Auto Layout, positioning views with manual frame math for speed
It's required whenever more than two views sit side by side
It removes the need for each label to report an intrinsic content size

questions.prompt: What does calling apply(_:animatingDifferences:) here actually do, compared to removing the item from a plain array and calling reloadData()?
questions.explanation: Diffable data sources compute the difference between the previous and new snapshot themselves — insertions, deletions, moves — and animate exactly that difference. reloadData(), by contrast, reconfigures every visible cell regardless of what actually changed.

options.text: It behaves like reloadData(), just with an animation curve layered on top
It requires manually calling beginUpdates()/endUpdates() first, like the older APIs
It diffs the snapshot against the current one, animating only the changed rows
It replaces the entire data source object with a new instance from the snapshot

questions.prompt: A view's constraints compile and activate with no runtime warning, but the view still has no well-defined width. What's actually going on?
questions.explanation: Ambiguous means Auto Layout has more than one mathematically valid layout satisfying every constraint at once — nothing conflicts, so nothing warns, but the system still has to arbitrarily pick a resulting width. That's distinct from unsatisfiable, where constraints actively contradict each other and Auto Layout does log a warning while breaking one of them.

options.text: This only happens when translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints defaults to true
Xcode's layout engine caches a prior width whenever a constraint set is incomplete
The view has a required constraint pinned to a superview that hasn't loaded yet
The constraints are ambiguous, since they're consistent but not fully determined

questions.prompt: A screen's layout is built entirely in code, with no XIB or storyboard involved. What's a fair trade-off of that choice versus using Interface Builder?
questions.explanation: Programmatic layout trades away Interface Builder's visual canvas for the ordinary benefits of code review: it diffs cleanly in source control and makes conditional or parameterized layout logic easy to add. There's no restriction against Auto Layout, no meaningful runtime speed difference, and nothing being removed from the SDK here.

options.text: No live preview while designing, but easier to review in a code diff
Programmatic UI cannot use Auto Layout at all, only frame-based positioning
Storyboards compile to noticeably faster-executing code than hand-written layout
XIBs and storyboards are being removed from UIKit in an upcoming release

questions.prompt: What would change if [weak self] were removed from this closure, assuming networkService retains the closure until the download completes?
questions.explanation: Without [weak self], the closure captures self strongly by default. As long as networkService holds onto that closure, self stays alive too — for a one-shot completion handler that's usually a delayed deallocation rather than a permanent leak, but it does mean the view controller can outlive its dismissal until the network call resolves.

options.text: Nothing — closures never capture self unless self. is written explicitly
self is captured strongly, delaying dealloc until the download finishes
The app crashes immediately at the call site with an unowned-reference error
self is still captured weakly, regardless of the closure's own capture list

questions.prompt: This view controller is dismissed, but Instruments still shows it alive minutes later. What's the most likely cause, given this code?
questions.explanation: A repeating Timer is kept alive by the run loop until something calls invalidate() on it, and this timer's closure captures self strongly with no [weak self]. Timer alive, closure retaining self, timer never invalidated — that combination is exactly what keeps the view controller from deallocating.

options.text: UIViewController subclasses are retained by UIKit itself until the whole app terminates, independent of timers
The Timer holds its closure strongly, capturing self, and is never invalidated
Timer.scheduledTimer keeps its target alive only until the first fire
The closure syntax used here isn't valid Swift and wouldn't compile

questions.prompt: A view controller registers an observer with NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(forName: .someUpdate, object: nil, queue: nil) { _ in self.reloadData() } in viewDidLoad, capturing self, and never calls removeObserver or discards the returned token. iOS 9 / macOS 10.11 added automatic observer removal on deinit for the older selector-based addObserver(_:selector:name:object:) API. What's the concrete risk with the block-based registration shown here?
questions.explanation: The automatic on-deinit cleanup Apple added in iOS 9 / macOS 10.11 applies to the selector-based addObserver(_:selector:name:object:) API. Block-based registrations via addObserver(forName:object:queue:using:) aren't covered by it — NotificationCenter keeps the block, and anything it captures, alive as part of the registration, so it keeps firing on future posts until removeObserver is called explicitly or the returned token is removed.

options.text: No risk — the same on-deinit removal introduced in iOS 9 for observer cleanup covers block-based registrations exactly like it covers the selector-based API
The code won't compile — addObserver(forName:object:queue:using:) is only valid when the observing object also registers through the selector-based API
NotificationCenter silently queues the notification until removeObserver is called, then delivers everything at once
That on-deinit removal only covers the selector-based API — this block registration keeps self retained and keeps firing until removeObserver is called explicitly

questions.prompt: SwiftUI re-renders the parent view several times while this ActivityIndicatorView stays on screen. How many times does makeUIView run across those re-renders?
questions.explanation: makeUIView is the one-time constructor for the underlying UIKit object; SwiftUI keeps that instance around across re-renders and calls updateUIView to reflect new state onto the same view, rather than tearing it down and rebuilding it every time.

options.text: Once per re-render — UIViewRepresentable fully rebuilds the view just like body does
Once — makeUIView creates the view; updateUIView handles later updates
Zero times — makeUIView only runs inside a NavigationStack
Twice — once to measure size, once to actually display it

questions.prompt: An existing UIKit app wants to add one new screen written entirely in SwiftUI, pushed onto an existing UINavigationController. What makes that possible?
questions.explanation: UIHostingController<Content> is a genuine UIViewController subclass that hosts a SwiftUI view's rendering — that's what makes it pushable, presentable, and embeddable anywhere a UIKit view controller is expected. UIViewRepresentable solves the opposite direction, wrapping a UIKit view for use inside SwiftUI.

options.text: Wrapping the SwiftUI view in a UIHostingController, itself a UIViewController that can be pushed like any other
SwiftUI views push directly onto a UINavigationController's stack — View already conforms to UIViewController itself, no wrapper needed
The whole app must be rewritten in SwiftUI before any single screen can adopt it
UIViewRepresentable, which converts a SwiftUI view into a UINavigationController-compatible object

questions.prompt: A UIViewRepresentable wraps a UISearchBar and needs to react to UISearchBarDelegate callbacks by updating a SwiftUI @Binding. Since the representable struct itself can't conform to a class-only delegate protocol, what's the conventional fix?
questions.explanation: UISearchBarDelegate requires a class instance, and UIViewRepresentable conformers are structs. The Coordinator — a small class produced by makeCoordinator() — is the standard bridge: it becomes the actual delegate, receives UIKit callbacks, and pushes updates into SwiftUI state through a binding or closure it holds.

options.text: Mark the representable struct as a class instead of a struct, so it conforms directly
A nested Coordinator class, from makeCoordinator(), conforms to the delegate protocol
Have the SwiftUI view itself conform to the delegate and act as the search bar's delegate
Poll the search bar's text property on a timer instead of using the delegate

questions.prompt: A storyboard button is connected to `@IBAction func didTapSave(_ sender: UIButton)`. What determines when this method actually runs?
questions.explanation: An @IBAction is a method Interface Builder can wire to a specific control event, such as Touch Up Inside for a button. The connection determines which event triggers it, and it fires every time that event occurs — not once, not on a timer, and not tied to viewDidLoad.

options.text: It runs automatically whenever viewDidLoad executes, tap or no tap
It runs once per second for as long as the button stays on screen
Whichever control event Interface Builder wires that connection to
It only runs the first time the button is tapped, then the connection expires

questions.prompt: Calling both setNeedsLayout() and layoutIfNeeded() back to back here — what does the second call actually add?
questions.explanation: setNeedsLayout() flags the view dirty for the next layout pass, which UIKit would otherwise perform later on its own schedule. layoutIfNeeded() checks that flag and, if set, runs the layout pass right away — useful when you need updated frames before an animation starts, rather than waiting for the next natural pass.

options.text: It's a no-op unless setNeedsLayout() was never called first
It marks the view as needing layout a second time, doubling the effect
It forces the layout pass to happen immediately instead of waiting
It schedules layoutSubviews() to run on a background thread for speed

questions.prompt: What has to stay true for this performBatchUpdates call to avoid a crash, that wouldn't matter if the code instead just called tableView.reloadData()?
questions.explanation: performBatchUpdates (and the older beginUpdates/endUpdates) require your row-level delete/insert/move calls to exactly match what actually happened to the underlying data — get the count or index paths wrong and it throws an NSInternalInconsistencyException. reloadData() has no such requirement: it re-reads the data source from scratch, at the cost of animating nothing.

options.text: The closure must run asynchronously on a background queue, or UIKit rejects it
The mutation and the table update must agree on which index paths changed
items must be an NSArray rather than a Swift Array for the API to accept it
deleteRows must be called before items.remove(at:), or the animation is skipped

questions.prompt: UIControl-based views (buttons, sliders, switches) have historically used target-action rather than closures for handling events. What's a genuine practical reason for that design, beyond simply predating Swift closures?
questions.explanation: Target-action decouples the event source from the handler through a loose (selector, target) pair rather than a captured closure — that lets several controls share one action method, or one control fan out to several targets, without each pairing owning its own closure allocation. It's an architectural choice, not a hard limitation on closures inside UIKit — later APIs do accept them directly, e.g. UIAction on iOS 14+.

options.text: One control can register multiple targets, or share one action across controls
UIControl subclasses cannot capture values inside a closure, a compiler limitation
Closures aren't supported inside any UIKit event-handling API, even today
Target-action runs noticeably faster at runtime than any closure-based callback
